Obesity Trend Comparison

A visual guide to adult obesity trends across countries and continents.

Package documentation website: https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-shro-ots/

Purpose

The question: How have adult obesity estimates changed over time, and how do those patterns compare across places?

Obesity Trend Quest is an R package with an interactive Shiny app for students, public-health analysts, and curious readers who want an approachable way to explore these trends. Choose a year range, then look at one country or area alongside the rest of its continent, compare a few countries or areas, or even compare continent averages. The graph shows how the estimates move, and the quick-read notes highlight how much each line changed between the first and last year you selected.

The app helps you spot patterns and ask better follow-up questions. It’s important to note that these estimates don’t explain why a trend changed or show that a specific change in policy may have caused it, so treat the comparisons as a starting point for discussion instead of a foundation.

What you can explore

  • One country vs. the rest of its continent: compare one country or area with the unweighted average for the other places in that continent.

  • Compare countries/areas: view 2–5 selected places.

  • Compare continents: view 2–5 continent averages.

Choose a year range to update the graph and its summary.

Data

Obesity Trend Quest comes with a prepared dataset called obesity_data, so the app can use it straight away. It covers 1980–2024 and has five fields: entity, code, year, obesity_pct, and region.

The adult-obesity estimates come from the WHO Global Health Observatory accessed through the Our World in Data adult obesity grapher.

Credit: World Health Organization – Global Health Observatory (2026) – with minor processing by Our World in Data.

The WHO data is listed as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The package’s R code has a separate MIT licence. Keep the data’s source README and metadata with it, and check them before reusing or redistributing the data.

A quick note on the numbers: they estimate the percentage of adults classified as obese, rather than counting people. The continent averages in this package are calculated across the included countries or areas, with every place counting equally regardless of population. So they help you compare places, but they aren’t estimates for the average person in a continent. In the country comparison, the selected country is left out of its continent average.

Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-shro-ots")

Launching 

obstrendquest::run_app()

The app uses compare_obesity_trend() to prepare the selected comparison. You can also call it directly:

utils::data("obesity_data", package = "obstrendquest")

obstrendquest::compare_obesity_trend(
  data = obesity_data,
  comparison_mode = "countries",
  selections = c("India", "Australia"),
  start_year = 1980,
  end_year = 1985
)

The function returns a table with year, series, and obesity_pct columns. Run ?compare_obesity_trend in R for details.
